articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a Venezuela-related designation removal on October 14, 2026.

This action follows previous guidance from OFAC in February 2024, which indicated that temporary sanctions relief for the Venezuelan oil and mining sectors, specifically General License (GL) 44, would not be renewed without progress towards a free and competitive 2024 presidential election.

The revocation of GL 43 in January 2024, which authorized transactions involving CVG Compania General de Mineria de Venezuela CA, further signaled a snapback of sanctions on Venezuela's oil and mining sectors.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026.
These designations are part of ongoing efforts by the U.S. Treasury to combat illicit finance and disrupt networks involved in narcotics trafficking and global terrorism.
Such actions aim to protect the U.S. financial system from abuse and to pressure individuals and entities that support these illicit activities.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) reached an $11,662,930 settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, for apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs.
These violations included apparent breaches of sanctions programs covering Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.
The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination that the apparent violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, with no reduction for remedial measures or cooperation.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, ICC Designation, and Burma Sanctions Removal
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026.
Concurrently, OFAC issued a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and associated General Licenses, alongside a Burma-related designation removal.

These actions reflect OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, addressing various foreign policy and national security objectives, including accountability for international bodies and adjustments to existing country-specific programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026.

General Licenses are issued to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs, often to facilitate humanitarian aid, certain financial transactions, or other specific activities.
This new license indicates a specific carve-out or authorization within the broader Russia sanctions regime, which has seen significant expansion since 2022.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026.
Concurrently, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License.
These actions underscore the U.S. government's continued pressure on Iran through sanctions, while also making adjustments to facilitate certain activities under the Russia sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Alert Warning Foreign Financial Institutions on Iran Sanctions, Amends FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an alert on October 5, 2026, warning foreign financial institutions (FFIs) that they could be targeted without advance notification for transacting with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions.
This alert is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' launched in August 2026, aimed at cutting off financial resources to the Iranian regime.
OFAC also amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) 156, removing language that previously indicated OFAC would generally contact an FFI before making a finding of sanctionable activity.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism Designations on October 2, 2026.
These designations target individuals and entities involved in supporting terrorist activities globally, aiming to disrupt their financial networks and limit their ability to operate.
Such actions are a critical component of the U.S. government's strategy to combat international terrorism and protect national security.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related and Transnational Criminal Organizations Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and designations updates, as well as a Transnational Criminal Organizations designation on October 1, 2026.
This action also included the publication of an Iran-related Determination and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question.

These measures aim to further restrict the Iranian regime's access to financial resources and to combat the activities of transnational criminal organizations that pose a threat to U.S. national security.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Removes Belarus, Narcotics, and Libya Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations designations on September 30, 2026.
Concurrently, OFAC removed designations related to Belarus, Counter Narcotics, and Libya.
These actions demonstrate OFAC's ongoing efforts to target evolving threats while also adjusting sanctions programs based on changing geopolitical landscapes and policy considerations.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil penalty of $11,662,930 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 13, 2026.
This penalty is part of a broader enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department for violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.
The violations included apparent breaches of sanctions programs related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC

This penalty is part of OFAC's enforcement efforts to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.
The specific details of the violations leading to this penalty were not immediately disclosed but are typically related to unauthorized transactions or dealings with sanctioned entities or regions.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,427,230 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on September 10, 2026.
This significant penalty underscores OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions regulations against individuals who violate U.S. foreign policy and national security objectives.
The specific nature of the individual's violations was not detailed in the public record but typically involves unauthorized transactions or dealings with sanctioned countries, entities, or persons.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
